title: Gray code
html:
Gray code is a binary numeral system where two successive values differ in only one bit.

Denote by G(n)G(n)G(n) the representation of the number nnn using the Gray code. The sequence of Gray codes for 3-bit numbers is: 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100, so G(4)=(110)2=6G(4) = (110)_2 = 6G(4)=(110)2​=6. For example, G(3)=(010)2G(3) = (010)_2G(3)=(010)2​ and G(4)=(110)2G(4) = (110)_2G(4)=(110)2​ differ at exactly one bit, the leftmost bit. Similarly, G(4)=(110)2G(4) = (110)_2G(4)=(110)2​ and G(5)=(111)2G(5) = (111)_2G(5)=(111)2​ differ at exactly one bit, the rightmost one. This is true for all successive numbers.

This code was invented by Frank Gray in 1953.

Finding Gray code

Let's look at the bits of number nnn and the bits of number G(n)G(n)G(n). Notice that iii-th bit of G(n)G(n)G(n) equals 1 only when iii-th bit of nnn equals 1 and i+1i + 1i+1-th bit equals 0 or the other way around (iii-th bit equals 0 and i+1i + 1i+1-th bit equals 1). Thus, G(n)=n⊕(n>>1)G(n) = n \oplus (n >> 1)G(n)=n⊕(n>>1): 

int g (int n) {
    return n ^ (n >> 1);
}

Finding inverse Gray code

Given Gray code ggg, restore the original number nnn.

We will move from the most significant bits to the least significant ones (the least significant bit has index 1 and the most significant bit has index kkk). The relation between the bits nin_ini​ of number nnn and the bits gig_igi​ of number ggg:

nk=gk,nk−1=gk−1⊕nk=gk⊕gk−1,nk−2=gk−2⊕nk−1=gk⊕gk−1⊕gk−2,nk−3=gk−3⊕nk−2=gk⊕gk−1⊕gk−2⊕gk−3,⋮\begin{align} n_k &= g_k, \\ n_{k-1} &= g_{k-1} \oplus n_k = g_k \oplus g_{k-1}, \\ n_{k-2} &= g_{k-2} \oplus n_{k-1} = g_k \oplus g_{k-1} \oplus g_{k-2}, \\ n_{k-3} &= g_{k-3} \oplus n_{k-2} = g_k \oplus g_{k-1} \oplus g_{k-2} \oplus g_{k-3}, \vdots \end{align}nk​nk−1​nk−2​nk−3​​=gk​,=gk−1​⊕nk​=gk​⊕gk−1​,=gk−2​⊕nk−1​=gk​⊕gk−1​⊕gk−2​,=gk−3​⊕nk−2​=gk​⊕gk−1​⊕gk−2​⊕gk−3​,⋮​​

The easiest way to write it in code is:

int rev_g (int g) {
  int n = 0;
  for (; g; g >>= 1)
    n ^= g;
  return n;
}

Practical applications

Gray codes have some useful applications, sometimes quite unexpected:

  • Gray code of nnn bits forms a Hamiltonian cycle on a hypercube, where each bit corresponds to one dimension.

  • Gray codes are used to minimize the errors in digital-to-analog signals conversion (for example, in sensors).

  • Gray code can be used to solve the Towers of Hanoi problem. Let nnn denote number of disks. Start with Gray code of length nnn which consists of all zeroes (G(0)G(0)G(0)) and move between consecutive Gray codes (from G(i)G(i)G(i) to G(i+1)G(i+1)G(i+1)). Let iii-th bit of current Gray code represent iii-th disk (the least significant bit corresponds to the smallest disk and the most significant bit to the biggest disk). Since exactly one bit changes on each step, we can treat changing iii-th bit as moving iii-th disk. Notice that there is exactly one move option for each disk (except the smallest one) on each step (except start and finish positions). There are always two move options for the smallest disk but there is a strategy which will always lead to answer: if nnn is odd then sequence of the smallest disk moves looks like f→t→r→f→t→r→...f \to t \to r \to f \to t \to r \to ...f→t→r→f→t→r→... where fff is the initial rod, ttt is the terminal rod and rrr is the remaining rod, and if nnn is even: f→r→t→f→r→t→...f \to r \to t \to f \to r \to t \to ...f→r→t→f→r→t→....

  • Gray codes are also used in genetic algorithms theory.
